question: What has to change in a project's delivery to adopt a robotic process?

answer.answer:
To adopt robotic assembly (PR4), the delivery arrangement itself is one of the cited requirements: the business model and work culture (RI12) have to change, although only 2 of the 50 coded cases carry that pairing. The practical levers are organisational rather than technical: early contractor involvement (CO11) and vertical integration (CO10) sit upstream of an integrated design-DFAB process (AT12), prefabrication (PR2) and highly standardised components (AT7) sit upstream of the robot work itself, and workforce training (RI6) is the near-universal demand behind human-robot interaction (CO6). Of the six cited requirements of robotic assembly only one, the robotic arm (RE2), is a machine; the rest are processes, attributes, a condition and a risk. Watch one in particular: the mobile factory (CO12) is a direct cited precondition of robotic assembly and is carried by none of the 50.

**What robotic assembly actually requires.** PR4 "Robotic assembly" carries a complete set of four inbound and six outbound cited edges, and 13 of the 50 coded cases draw on it [1]. Its requirements, reading each relation by direction rather than by arrow head, are: a robotic arm, PR4 dependsOn RE2, carried by 12 of the 50 [1]; prefabrication, PR4 hasPrecondition PR2, carried by 4 [1]; highly standardised components, AT7 enablesCapability PR4, carried by 10, on the evidence of Japanese automated erection systems [1]; path-planning, PR12 enablesCapability PR4, carried by 2 [1]; the mobile factory, CO12 enablesCapability PR4, carried by 0 of the 50 [1]; and the delivery model, PR4 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", carried by 2, on the argument that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context (DEP61, peer-reviewed) [1]. The asymmetry is the finding: the robot arm is carried ten times more often than the delivery-model requirement or the path-planning one, and the mobile factory condition is not exhibited at all, even though 1 of the 50 cases draws on CO12 in its own right [1]. In their own right the counts are far from flat: 22 of the 50 draw on RE2 [1], 25 on AT7 [1], 26 on PR12 [1], 20 on PR2 [1] and 16 on RI12 [1].

**The delivery-side change.** RI12 is reached by exactly two cited edges and sends none. Besides DEP61 from robotic assembly, AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn RI12, carried by 13 of the 50, on the argument that adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [1]. That contrast is useful: the literature ties business-model change much more firmly to industrialisation at scale than to a single robotic assembly operation.

**What changes in the contract and the team.** The cited paths into an integrated process are three. Vertical integration enablesCapability AT12, carried by 14 of the 50 [1], and the mirroring argument runs the other way as AT12 hasPrecondition CO10, also carried by 14: technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm [1]. Early contractor involvement enablesCapability AT12, carried by 10 [1], and a DFAB design coordinator (AC4) enablesCapability AT12, carried by 7 [1]. CO11 is the most productive lever in this set, with three outbound edges in all: beyond AT12 it reaches prefabrication, carried by 13, because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and a delivery method that does so must be selected [1], and DfMA for DFAB (PR9), carried by 11 [1]. 14 of the 50 draw on CO11 [1] and 25 on CO10 [1], so vertical integration is the commoner state while early involvement is the more contractually available move.

**Workforce and compliance.** CO6 "Human-robot interaction" is drawn on by 32 of the 50 [1] and carries three outbound edges. CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", carried by 27 of the 50, the heaviest carried edge in this material, on the finding that human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1]. CO6 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", carried by 2, against robot safety standards [1], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern", carried by 4, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation [1]. Training is the change almost every project has to make: 44 of the 50 draw on RI6 [1]. Note that RI20's total edge count is 3 and only CO6's is listed here, so nothing can be said about how many paths reach it overall.

**Scheduling and the process model.** PR18 "Lean" hasPrecondition AR14 "Task schedule planning", carried by 13 of the 50, because production with short takt requires a highly detailed definition of tasks to avoid ambiguousness [1], so the schedule artefact is upstream of the lean process. 28 of the 50 draw on AR14 [1] and 21 on PR18 [1]. Two enablers here carry no cited edge but matter to the question: AT11 "Sequential design-DFAB process" is drawn on by 19 of the 50 and has no dependency edge [1], the same count as AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process", also 19 [1], which says the integrated model has not displaced the sequential one in the record; and RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" is drawn on by 17 of the 50 with no cited edge at all [1], the price of the standardisation that AT7 requires, simply not connected by the literature yet.

**What the deployed records show.** The retrieved census processes are all assembly-adjacent and all at high readiness, and their stated adoption drivers bear directly on the delivery question. census_RXT35-1, from Firm_109, performs assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting on the structural core and the building envelope, was adopted to address cost and safety, and is at technology readiness level 9 [1] [2]. census_RXH7-2, from Firm_125 and a census record of process RP29, performs assembly and tiling on the envelope, adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market, at technology readiness level 9 [3]. census_RXH4-1, from Firm_166, performs assembly and concrete work on the structural core and envelope, adopted to address cost and labor, at technology readiness level 9 [4]. Labor and cost recur across these records, which matches the training and business-model pressure the edges describe. One limit to state plainly: this context links the census records to firms, materials and parent processes only, so it does not say which enablers any of these cases draws on, and none of the counts above can be attributed to them individually.

**Reading the evidence.** Every relation above is a directional dependency, not correlation; the only correlational material here is the co-occurrence list, of which 1878 edges touch these enablers and only the 15 strongest are shown [1]. The cited dependency layer is sparse, 100 edges touching 68 of the 140 enablers, which is a property of the literature and not of the record [1], so an absent edge is not an absent requirement. Retrieval also read "delivery" narrowly as RI12, so contractual instruments beyond the enablers named here are outside what this answer can claim.
